title: Should Christians Drink Alcohol?
excerpt: The Bible calls wine a gift, warns against it in some of its most vivid lines, and honors people who never touch it. Christians who abstain and Christians who drink in moderation each have Scripture and a long history, and Romans 14 gives both of them an order.
body:
A man eleven years sober stands at his niece's wedding with a glass of sparkling juice, and a cousin asks him, kindly enough, whether he really thinks that is what Jesus made at Cana. A young woman grew up in a church where no member drank and now belongs to one where the men's group meets at a brewery, and she can't tell which congregation misled her. A third person has never liked the smell of whiskey, because of what came home with it when she was nine, and she has stopped trying to explain that to friends who think her rule against it is a leftover from a stricter age.

The skeptic watching all this has a fair comment. Here is a religion whose founder provided the wine at a wedding and whose central meal includes a cup, and a large part of it has spent two centuries urging its members never to touch one. Christians, he says, cannot even agree about dinner.

Some people come to this question because they are worried about their own drinking, or someone else's. For them the argument can wait. If drinking has become hard to control, you do not have to face it alone. Tell someone you trust, and reach out to a doctor or a recovery group near you. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. The page there for the person who [can't stop drinking or using](/help/addiction) is the place to start.

## What the Bible Says About Wine

The Bible says three things about wine, and most arguments on the subject are won by quoting one of them and leaving out the other two.

It calls wine a gift. A psalm that thanks God for grass, bread and oil thanks him also for "wine to gladden the heart of man" (Psalm 104:15). The law told Israel to bring "wine or strong drink" to the feast and rejoice before the Lord (Deuteronomy 14:26). Isaiah pictures the end of all sorrow as a banquet with "well-aged wine" (Isaiah 25:6). Jesus' first sign was wine for a village wedding, and the steward's only complaint was about the timing: "you have kept the good wine until now" (John 2:10). His enemies called him "a glutton and a drunkard" (Luke 7:34). The charge was a lie, but nobody would have thought to bring it against a man who never drank. Paul told a younger pastor, "use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments" (1 Timothy 5:23).

It also warns, and the warnings are among the most vivid passages in Scripture. The first story after the flood is of Noah, who "drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent" (Genesis 9:21). "Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler" (Proverbs 20:1). Proverbs 23 describes the red wine sparkling in the cup and says, "In the end it bites like a serpent and stings like an adder" (Proverbs 23:32). The passage closes inside the drinker's own head: "When shall I awake? I must have another drink" (Proverbs 23:35). That is a picture of addiction, written many centuries before anyone had a clinical word for it. Paul puts it as a command, "do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery" (Ephesians 5:18), and he lists drunkenness among the things that shut a person out of the kingdom (Galatians 5:21).

And it honors people who never touch it. The Nazirite vow required a man or woman to "separate himself from wine and strong drink" (Numbers 6:3). John the Baptist drank none from birth. When Jeremiah set pitchers of wine in front of the family of the Rechabites, they answered, "We will drink no wine" (Jeremiah 35:6), because an ancestor had forbidden it, and God set their obedience beside Judah's disobedience and promised the family a future. Timothy himself seems to have been drinking only water until Paul told him otherwise.

So the gift, the warning and the honored abstainer all stand in the same book. Some defenders of abstinence have argued that the wine Scripture approves was unfermented. The page on this site about [alcohol and drinking](/wisdom/alcohol-and-drinking) reports that most scholars think the wine at Cana was real wine, the ordinary drink of a feast, usually mixed with water. The case for abstaining does not need the weaker argument, and its best advocates have not rested on it.

## The Case for Moderation

Most Christians in most centuries have held that wine is a good creature of God and that the sin lies in its abuse. That is the teaching of the Catholic and Orthodox churches and of the Lutheran, Anglican and Reformed traditions, and for most of the church's history the cup at the Lord's Table held wine.

The argument is older than any of those names. In the year 387 John Chrysostom was preaching in Antioch on Paul's advice to Timothy, and he turned on certain Christians in his own congregation who, seeing drunkards disgrace themselves, had begun to say, "Let there be no wine." His answer has been repeated ever since: "Let there be no drunkenness; for wine is the work of God, but drunkenness is the work of the devil." He was not soft on the drunkard, whom he called in the same sermon "a living corpse." His point was about where the blame belongs. To condemn the thing God made, he said, is to insult the giver.

Those who hold this view point to Paul. "Everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving" (1 Timothy 4:4). "Let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink" (Colossians 2:16). And they point especially to his warning about rules that sound devout: "Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch" has "an appearance of wisdom," he wrote, but such rules "are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh" (Colossians 2:21, 23).

What they fear is a commandment God never gave. A church that forbids what Scripture permits has put its own judgment above the Bible's, however good its motive. They add, from long observation, that a rule does not cure a heart. Forbidden drinking can simply move to where no one sees it, and the abstainer's pride can do as much harm as the drinker's glass.

## The Case for Abstaining

The other view is just as old in its instinct. Around the year 200 Clement of Alexandria, who thought wine lawful for grown men and women, wrote, "I therefore admire those who have adopted an austere life, and who are fond of water, the medicine of temperance, and flee as far as possible from wine, shunning it as they would the danger of fire." He told the young to keep away from it altogether.

What turned that instinct into a movement was a change in the drink. The wine of the Bible was fermented, and usually watered. Distilled spirits, which are far stronger, are a much later invention. When John Wesley preached on the use of money in the eighteenth century, he was not speaking of wine when he condemned "that liquid fire, commonly called drams or spirituous liquors," and said that those who sold it to anyone who would buy were "poisoners-general." The physician Benjamin Rush, whose tract on the subject the American Tract Society kept in print, drew the same line in his first sentence: "By ardent spirits, I mean those liquors only which are obtained by distillation."

The temperance movement of the nineteenth century began there, as a campaign against spirits, and grew into a pledge against all alcohol. It is often remembered now as a crusade of the prim. The people in it described something else. Their tracts tell of wages spent before they reached home and of men who could no longer support their families. In December of 1873 women in small towns in New York and Ohio organized to carry an appeal to the liquor dealers of their towns, and called it the Woman's Crusade. The following year they formed the Woman's Christian Temperance Union. The record of its New York branch shows what else those women were working for: among the laws it lists as won is one that raised the age of consent from ten years to sixteen. These were women with little standing in law, defending their households with the tools they had.

Their appeal to Scripture was mainly to love, and they did not need to claim that wine was evil. A tract of the period bases its case on the duty to "give no occasion of stumbling to any brother." Paul had written, "It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble" (Romans 14:21), and "'All things are lawful for me,' but I will not be dominated by anything" (1 Corinthians 6:12). In a society where a share of all who drink will be destroyed by it, and nobody knows in advance who, the abstainer gives up a pleasure so that the endangered person is never the only one at the table without a glass. Churches in the Baptist, Methodist, Holiness and Pentecostal families have long taught or encouraged this.

What they fear is a liberty that costs its owner nothing and someone else everything. They have buried too many people to be charmed by talk of Christian freedom over a good bottle.

The movement's largest victory was also its hardest lesson. For thirteen years in the last century the sale of alcohol was forbidden across the United States, and then the ban was repealed. Whether a conviction of conscience should be made everyone's law is a separate question from whether the conviction is right, and Christians who abstain have answered it both ways.

## The Weaker Brother

Both sides claim Romans 14, and both are right to, because Paul wrote it to two groups at once.

The quarrel in Rome was over food and holy days. Some believers ate anything, and some, out of scruple, ate "only vegetables" (Romans 14:2). Paul addresses each party with a different command. "Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him" (Romans 14:3). Contempt is the temptation of the free, and condemnation is the temptation of the strict. He forbids both in one sentence. Then he asks a question that applies to each: "Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another?" (Romans 14:4).

The harder demand falls on the person who is free. "If your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died" (Romans 14:15). The words are strong, and they show what Paul means by stumbling. He is not describing a fellow Christian who merely disapproves, or who would be irritated to see a wine list. A person who stumbles falls. The brother in view is someone who would be drawn by another's example into what will wreck him, or into acting against his own conscience, since "whatever does not proceed from faith is sin" (Romans 14:23).

In our setting that person is easy to find. He is the guest in his first year of sobriety, or the teenager watching how the adults in the church handle a drink. She is the friend who has never said why she turns down the glass. Paul does not tell the free that their freedom is false. He agrees with them that "nothing is unclean in itself" (Romans 14:14). He tells them that love outranks it.

The abstainer has to hear Paul too. He is welcomed, "but not to quarrel over opinions" (Romans 14:1), and he has no right to treat his own practice as the measure of another person's faith. Each of them is told the same thing: "The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord," and "the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord" (Romans 14:6).

## When It Is Not a Question of Freedom

For some people none of this is a debate about liberty. The drink has stopped being a choice.

The Bible knows this condition. The voice at the end of Proverbs 23 wants another drink before the bruises from the last one have healed. Paul's list of those who will not inherit the kingdom includes "drunkards," and the next sentence may be the most hopeful in the letter: "And such were some of you" (1 Corinthians 6:11). There were recovering drunkards in the church at Corinth, and Paul counted them among the washed.

The site's page for people in this place says plainly that "addiction lives in the body," and that a pastor and a church cannot manage it alone. It also carries a warning that matters more than anything in this essay: "if you drink or use every day, don't quit suddenly on your own; stopping alcohol and some other drugs can be dangerous." A doctor is the first call. This essay is not medical advice, and it can't counsel anyone. [Find Help](/help) is where the site keeps the places to turn, for the person who drinks and for the family that lives with it.

The church has failed such people from both sides of this argument. Where abstinence is the rule, we have often made a drinking problem impossible to confess, because the confession would have to start with the admission that one drank at all, and so people have gone under in silence in the strictest congregations. Where liberty is prized, we have made the sober man feel like a scold for declining, pressed a glass on a guest whose history we never asked about, and built our fellowship around the one thing he cannot be near. Each side has been certain that the other was the one doing the damage.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Some of this is settled. Drunkenness is sin, and Scripture never treats it lightly. Wine is something God made, and Scripture never calls it evil. No Christian may despise another for abstaining or condemn another for drinking. The person who is trapped is owed help, without contempt, and so is the family.

Whether a Christian should drink at all is a question of the third order. Scripture leaves it to conscience, faithful churches have answered it both ways for good reasons, and this essay takes no side. Paul's rule covers both answers: "whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God" (1 Corinthians 10:31).

There is one more abstainer in the New Testament. On the night of his arrest Jesus took the cup, gave it to his friends, and said, "I tell you I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom" (Matthew 26:29). He is waiting for a table where no one will have reason to fear what is poured. The man at his niece's wedding is not at that table yet, and neither is the cousin who teased him. Until they are, each of them will answer to the same Lord for what he did with his glass, and for whether he noticed who was sitting beside him.

*"Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him."* (Romans 14:3)

*"I tell you I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom."* (Matthew 26:29)
